facts.text: Roma sits on a bluff above the Rio Grande, founded as a Spanish colony and now hosts a nine‑block historic plaza with over 30 pre‑1900 buildings.
The Roma National Historic Landmark District, designated in 1993, includes the 1840 Leocadia Garcia House, once a home, store, and dance hall.
German architect Heinrich Portscheller’s brickwork, with rounded corners and carved motifs, gives many Roma residences a distinctive European flair.
Roma’s river wharfs and old customs house were key to steamboat trade, where shippers paid fees for goods arriving from across the border.
The town survived railroad bypasses, preserving its 18th‑century layout and making it a living snapshot of early Texan frontier life.
In the 1950s, Roma served as the fictional “Rosita’s Cantina” in the film Viva Zapata, filmed on its historic streets.
